structure.rationale: The order follows how a fork-based risk engine is built and used: first the market objects it prices off (curves and conventions), then what it measures on them (risk measures), the instruments it holds (Treasuries, futures, SOFR swaps), and the time/funding effects that move value without a market move (carry, roll, funding). Liquidity and scenarios then say what trading costs and which futures to test; hedging and optimization turn those into trades; data operations and governance cover feeding the engine and trusting its output. Chapters are the requester's nine, kept in their order; each is told as one scene in plain words per the Thing Explainer voice, with the real term quoted once.
structure.audience: A team building a fixed-income fork-based risk engine, assumed to know bonds and swaps at a working level but needing the trading-desk and bank-governance context around them.
structure.status: skeleton: sources are structure anchors named in book.json notes plus primary-data/docs pointers; URLs and claims are to be verified by each concept step before use

claims.text: US Treasury notes and bonds use Actual/Actual (ICMA): accrued fraction = actual days since last coupon / (days in coupon period x coupons per year); a 182-day half-year gives a 364 denominator.

SOFR fixed-vs-floating swaps trade with annual payments on both legs, both ACT/360 (fixed leg too). The 30/360 semi-annual fixed leg is the legacy LIBOR-era convention; cleared venues permit other fixed day counts, so confirm per trade.
Brief lists 30/360 for fixed swap legs; for SOFR swaps the market convention is ACT/360 annual, so the page teaches 30/360 as the older/other-currency convention and flags the difference.
Log-linear interpolation of discount factors is the same as piecewise-constant forward rates between nodes (forwards jump at nodes).

Monotone convex (Hagan & West) keeps continuous forwards positive when input discrete forwards are positive and preserves monotonicity regions; it reproduces each period's discrete forward by integration.
Dirty price = clean price + accrued interest; Treasuries trade on clean price and regular-way settle next business day (T+1) — common market practice, not confirmed from a fetched primary source.
Treasury publishes a daily par yield curve (CMT) at fixed tenors from on-the-run securities; fitted-spline approaches use all bonds.
SOFR is a published overnight rate; SOFR OIS compounds it daily and is the standard USD discounting curve for cleared swaps.
QuantLib objects: YieldTermStructure (curve base), RelinkableYieldTermStructureHandle, SimpleQuote, Observer/Observable; curves are LazyObject and recompute when a quote changes.

snippets.code:
q = ql.SimpleQuote(0.0425)
h = ql.QuoteHandle(q)
helper = ql.OISRateHelper(2, ql.Period('5Y'), h, sofr_index)
curve = ql.PiecewiseLogLinearDiscount(today, [helper], ql.Actual365Fixed())
handle = ql.RelinkableYieldTermStructureHandle(curve)
q.setValue(0.0430)  # curve notices, rebuilds on next query
snippets.note: Pattern from QuantLib docs/cookbook; not executed here — check class names against installed QuantLib version.

pitfalls: Using ACT/360 vs ACT/ACT for a quote moves rates by roughly 1.4% of the rate — silently wrong carry.
Accrued interest uses coupon-period length, so it differs between semiannual periods of 181-184 days.
Log-linear discount interpolation gives sawtooth forwards; bumping one node shifts forwards unevenly.
Forgetting that a 'next business day' settlement date changes accrued interest on Fridays/holidays.
Relinking a handle changes every dependent instrument — intended for forks, but easy to share by accident.

claims.text: DV01 = modified duration x price x 0.0001: the dollar value change for a one basis point move. Sign convention varies; state it (here: DV01 is the loss for +1bp, positive for a long bond).
Portfolio DV01 is the sum of position DV01s when all use the same parallel shift of the same curve; it hides offsetting exposures at different tenors.
Key-rate DV01 uses a triangular bump peaking at a key tenor and tapering linearly to neighbours, estimated by central difference (P- minus P+) / 2; partial durations sum to the parallel duration.
Bumping par (market quote) rates and re-bootstrapping gives risk per instrument a trader can hedge; bumping zero rates gives risk per curve node. Choice is a convention that must be stated.

Duration and convexity are the first two Taylor terms; accuracy falls as shock size grows; sources suggest adding convexity beyond ~25-50bp, and full revaluation for large shocks, curve-shaped scenarios and optionality.
Bump size must be small enough to be local but large enough to avoid numerical noise; 1bp central difference is a common convention, not a rule.
Hedging with DV01 alone removes first-order parallel risk only; convexity and curve-shape risk remain.
Curve-shape shocks: bull/bear = yields down/up; steepener/flattener = long-minus-short spread widens/narrows; butterfly = belly moves vs wings. Level, slope, curvature are the usual PCA factors.
P&L attribution splits change in value into carry, roll-down, curve move, spread change and an unexplained residual.

snippets.code: 10y, 4% semiannual coupon bond at 4% yield, price 100: DV01 = 0.0818 per 100 face; convexity ~ 78.9 (in yield-squared units, per 100 price: 7889.8/100); +25bp: full -2.0195, DV01-only -2.0439, DV01+convexity -2.0193; +100bp: full -7.7946, DV01-only -8.1757, with convexity -7.7812; +200bp: full -14.877, DV01-only -16.351, with convexity -14.773.
snippets.note: Computed by the author in Python from the bond price formula on 2026-10-08.

pitfalls: Mixing sign conventions between systems flips hedges.
Summing DV01 across currencies/curves without a common curve.
Bumping zero rates when the desk hedges with par instruments.
Too-small bumps give noise; one-sided bumps bias with convexity.
Taylor on instruments with optionality or large curve-shape shocks.
Residual in attribution is a signal of a bug, not noise to hide.

claims.text: Treasury marketable securities are bills (a year or less, sold at a discount), notes (2 to 10 years), bonds (20 and 30 years), TIPS and FRNs; bills are auctioned on a weekly cadence (e.g. 13- and 26-week usually Mondays).
Auctions are announced in advance; noncompetitive bids are filled first, then competitive bids from lowest yield up; all winners get the highest accepted yield (single-price).
When-issued trading happens between announcement and issue: dealers sell the new security ahead of the auction, giving bidders a price signal.
STRIPS are zero-coupon pieces made by separating a note/bond/TIPS into individual coupon and principal payments (a 10y note becomes 21 pieces); held and traded via dealers, not TreasuryDirect.

On-the-run vs off-the-run: the most recently auctioned issue of a maturity trades richer and more liquid; the gap is a liquidity premium that varies with market stress and with age of the issue. (General market knowledge; no single primary source fetched.)

CME lists 2-year (face $200k), 5-year, 10-year, Ultra 10-year, U.S. Bond (codes TU, FV, TY, US named in the brief; Ultra codes unverified) and Ultra Bond futures, face $100k except 2y. Deliverable maturities: 2y 1¾–2y (original term ≤5¼y), 5y 4 1/6–5¼y, 10y 6½–8y per CBOT table (newer CME whitepaper says up to 10y), Ultra 10y 9 5/12–10y, Bond 15–25y, Ultra Bond 25–30y. The brief also lists UB and WN as the two 'ultra' codes; exchange code naming (Globex vs clearing) was not verified, so the page avoids assigning them.
Ticks: 10y and Ultra 10y 1/2 of 1/32 ($15.625); Bond and Ultra Bond 1/32 ($31.25); 5y 1/4 of 1/32 ($7.8125); 2y 1/8 of 1/32 ($15.625). Quarterly Mar/Jun/Sep/Dec cycle; physical delivery.

Conversion factor restates each deliverable bond's price as if it yielded 6%; invoice price = futures settlement × CF + accrued interest. The 6% convention favors some bonds, which is why a CTD exists.

Gross basis = cash price − futures price × CF. Net basis = gross basis − carry (coupon accrual less financing). The CTD has the lowest net basis, equivalently the highest implied repo rate (CME QuikStrike words it as the top row by implied repo; check sign convention in source).
Implied repo rate is the financing rate that makes buying the bond and delivering into the future break even; day-count 360 for USTs.
Futures DV01 ≈ CTD DV01 / CF; when yields move the CTD can switch, abruptly changing the contract's effective duration (CTD switch risk).

Delivery options for the short: quality (which bond), timing (which day in the delivery month), end-of-month option, and the wild card (futures settle 2pm Chicago, short may declare delivery until later in the evening; sources differ 7pm vs 8pm).

SOFR OIS swaps: annual payments both legs, ACT/360, New York calendar, 2-business-day payment lag; floating leg is compounded daily SOFR over the period; lookback/lag exists because the last fixing is published the next day.

LCH cleared first SOFR swaps in 2018; CME moved discounting/PAI to SOFR in 2018, LCH moved to SOFR discounting in Oct 2020. Cleared swaps are margined by the CCP; swap default auction horizon up to five days (longer than futures' one day, so swap IM is higher than for equivalent futures).

Swap spread = swap rate minus Treasury yield of same maturity; it has been negative at long maturities for years. Drivers cited: dealer balance-sheet limits (eSLR), liability-driven receive-fixed demand, Treasury supply/fiscal outlook, LIBOR-to-SOFR transition removing a credit premium. The eSLR recalibration was adopted in Nov 2025.

snippets.code: Illustrative only: CTD DV01 = 0.0700 per 100 face, CF = 0.8000 -> future DV01 per 100 face-of-futures = 0.0700/0.8000 = 0.0875; one $100k contract = $87.50 per bp.
snippets.note: Made-up numbers to show the division, not market data.

pitfalls: Dividing by CF gives CTD-based DV01 only while that bond stays CTD; recompute after a switch.
Confusing sign: highest implied repo = lowest net basis = CTD.
Using stale contract specs (10y deliverable range, ticks) — fetch live from CME.
Treating a swap spread's sign as 'credit risk'; it is mostly funding, balance-sheet and supply.
Mixing the fixed-leg ACT/360 SOFR convention with old 30/360 LIBOR-era fixed legs.

claims.text: Carry is income from holding a bond (coupon accrual) minus the cost of financing it; it can be positive or negative depending on curve level and slope.

Roll-down is the price gain from a bond aging to a shorter maturity along an unchanged, upward-sloping curve; it is largest where the curve is steepest. Total return = carry + roll-down + price change from curve moves.
The 'unchanged curve' assumption is hard to satisfy in Treasuries because yields are volatile, so carry+roll is a baseline, not a forecast.
A common breakeven: the yield rise over the horizon that wipes out carry plus roll-down, approximately (carry + roll) / DV01. Conventions differ on funding and reinvestment, so state them.

Implied repo rate (IRR) is the financing return embedded in the cash/futures relationship: buy cash, sell futures, deliver. It is not quoted in the repo market. The bond with the highest IRR is the CTD; lowest net basis usually picks the same bond.

Net basis = gross basis - carry; gross basis = cash price - futures price x conversion factor. If IRR exceeds your actual repo rate, the cash-and-carry trade looks attractive before costs and delivery options.

General collateral (GC) repo is driven by funding costs; special repo is driven by demand for a specific security. Specials trade below GC, so owning the special bond lowers your financing cost and raises carry.

The TMPG fails charge is max(3% - reference rate, 0) per annum, so it caps the fail-driven part of specialness at 3% only when rates are below 3%; securities have occasionally traded through it. Verify the current formula before use.

A fixed-vs-SOFR swap's carry is the fixed rate received (or paid) minus the expected floating SOFR; at an unchanged curve the floating leg is assumed to reset at forwards, so swap carry is the fixed rate minus the forward rate over the period plus roll-down on the swap's remaining life.

Time-roll shock in a fork engine: advance the valuation date by the horizon while holding the market curve (or its forwards) fixed, reprice, and compare; the difference minus accrual is roll-down. Whether the curve is held in 'rates at constant tenor' or 'forwards realized' changes the answer; state which.

snippets.code: 5y 4% semiannual note, par (price 100), yield 4.00%, curve slopes 20bp per year at the 5y point (made up). Financing 3.60% on 100 for 1 month. Carry: coupon accrual 0.3333 - financing 0.3000 = 0.0333. Roll-down: 1m later 4y11m yield 3.9833%, clean price gain 0.0710. Total 0.1044 per 100. DV01 ~0.0443 per 100 per bp so breakeven ~2.4bp.
snippets.note: Computed by the author in Python on 2026-10-08 from the bond price formula; illustrative inputs.

pitfalls: Reporting dirty-price change as roll-down: accrual is carry, not roll.
Using GC repo for a bond that trades special.
Quoting carry as annualised without saying the day count (ACT/360 financing vs coupon basis).
Treating carry+roll as a forecast.
Mixing signs: carry drag of a hedge is a cost to a trader; say per month in dollars.

claims.text: Quoted bid-offer spread is the implied cost of liquidity and the usual first liquidity proxy: wider means less liquid. Dispersion across dealer quotes is a second signal.
Spread is a half-cost for a small trade: a round trip pays the full spread, a one-way trade about half of it, before any size effect.
On-the-run securities are under 4% of outstanding Treasury debt but about 65% of average daily trading volume (TRACE, Jun 2026 post, mainly 2-year notes).
As Treasuries age, volume and trade frequency fall, trade size rises, and effective bid-ask spreads widen. Exception: bonds cheapest to deliver into futures trade more than similar-age off-the-runs.
Quoted spreads can stay tight in stress while depth and volume deteriorate, so spread alone understates liquidity risk; depth and size-at-the-touch matter too.

SOFR swap bid-offer spreads tightened through 2021 to below LIBOR equivalents; Bloomberg put SOFR at 73% of USD swap volume on its venues by Jan 2022. Tradeweb SEF carried 52% of SEF SOFR notional and 71% of dealer-to-client SOFR notional in Q1 2022 (dated figures).

Square-root law: average price impact of a large order of size Q rises roughly with volatility times sqrt(Q / daily volume), exponent typically 0.4-0.7 and near 0.5, constant of order one. Mostly estimated on equities and futures; applying it to Treasuries or swaps needs calibration to your own data and is an assumption.

TRACE: Treasury trades are reported to FINRA and public on a next-day basis; public dissemination covers on-the-run nominal coupons with large-trade size capping; Treasury (2026) is asking whether one-hour delay would be better. Treasury credits transparency, electronic trading and buybacks with lower average transaction costs.

BrokerTec CLOB (New York) is the interdealer central limit order book and primary price-discovery venue for cash Treasuries (Feb 2025 ADNV $113bn). A second Chicago CLOB launched 6 Oct 2025 for relative-value trading, with smaller sizes and tighter increments to match futures.

Dealer-to-client Treasury trading is mostly request-for-quote (RFQ) on platforms such as Tradeweb and Bloomberg; interdealer is mostly CLOB. Share-of-volume figures found were dated (2020) and unverified, so the page gives no percentages.
CME 10-year note futures: $100,000 face; tick 1/2 of 1/32 point = $15.625; calendar-spread tick 1/4 of 1/32 = $7.8125. 30-year bond: 1/32 = $31.25. Chapter 3 gives the other ticks.

Futures trade in whole contracts only, so a hedge computed as 313.4 contracts must be rounded; block-trade minimums exist (10-year about 5,000 in regular hours per CME quick reference; sources for the bond differ 2,000 vs 3,000) and should be read live from CME.
Cleared swaps pay no bid-ask on a cash price but on a rate: a quoted spread in basis points on the swap rate, converted to dollars via the trade's DV01.

snippets.code:
cost_usd = half_spread_bp * dv01_usd + impact_bp * dv01_usd   # bp x $/bp
n_contracts = round(target_dv01 / fut_dv01)           # whole contracts only

pitfalls: Treating the quoted spread as the full cost for large size.
Using one spread for all tenors or all ages of the same maturity bucket.
Black-box liquidity score nobody can explain: every input should be shown with its raw value.
Quoting dated venue market shares or block minimums as fact; read from CME/venue live.
Rounding futures per-trade without checking the leftover DV01 after rounding.

claims.text: The FOMC holds eight scheduled meetings a year. In 2026: Jan 27-28, Mar 17-18, Apr 28-29, Jun 16-17, Jul 28-29, Sep 15-16, Oct 27-28, Dec 8-9.

The statement and rate decision come out at 2:00 pm ET on the second day; the Chair's press conference follows at 2:30 pm ET. The Summary of Economic Projections (with the dot plot) accompanies the March, June, September and December meetings only.
The dot plot shows each participant's anonymous view of the appropriate policy rate at year-ends and the longer run. It is a set of individual projections, not a committee commitment.
The policy rate directly anchors the front end; the long end reflects the expected path of policy plus term premium, so a surprise usually moves 2-year yields more than 10- or 30-year yields.

Hawkish surprise (higher expected path) typically gives a bear flattener: short yields up more than long yields. Dovish surprise typically gives a bull steepener: short yields fall more than long yields. Bull/bear refer to price direction; flattener/steepener to the 2s10s spread. A bear steepener (long end up more, e.g. term-premium or supply fears) and a bull flattener (long end rallies more, e.g. growth scare) are the other two.

Other scheduled drivers: CPI and the Employment Situation (payrolls, normally first Friday) are monthly BLS releases at 8:30 am ET; Treasury announces its quarterly refunding in early Feb/May/Aug/Nov, and auctions of 3-, 10- and 30-year securities follow; auction tails/stops-through move the sector.

2013 taper tantrum: after Bernanke's May 2013 hint of slowing asset purchases, the 10-year yield rose from about 1.6-1.7% in early May to about 3.0% by early September (roughly 100 bp in seven weeks, ~130-150 bp over five months). Sources differ on the exact start level; the spread behaviour was not measured in the sources found, so do not call it a clean steepener.

2022 hiking cycle: the funds target went from 0-0.25% (Mar 2022) to 5.25-5.50% (Jul 2023), 525 bp total. The curve bear-flattened and 2s10s inverted: first briefly in late March 2022, and deeply in 2022-23 (about -100 bp, the deepest since 1981). Early-2022 example: 2-year +156 bp vs 10-year +81 bp.

Replaying a historical scenario means applying the observed key-rate changes between two dates to today's curve and fully repricing; it is plausible by construction but only covers shapes that happened.

PCA on yield-curve changes (Litterman-Scheinkman 1991): the first three components are level, slope and curvature and explain nearly all variance (published figures range about 85-95% for level and 99%+ for three together, depending on sample and maturities).

Hypothetical scenario design: shock the factors (e.g. 'level +50 bp, slope -20 bp') and map back to tenors via loadings; that keeps tenors consistent and avoids implausible kinks. Choose size in standard deviations of the factor over a stated horizon.

CCAR/DFAST: the Fed publishes baseline and severely adverse scenarios each year. The 2026 severely adverse scenario has the 3-month Treasury yield falling from 3.7% (end 2025) to 0.1% within two quarters, unemployment up 5.5 points to a 10% peak, GDP down 4.6%, equities down 58%. The 2026 baseline holds the 10-year near 4.1%. A stated severely adverse 10-year path was not found.

pitfalls: Calling every rise in yields 'hawkish' flattening: supply or term-premium shocks steepen.
Shocking tenors independently produces kinks and negative forwards; use a factor or smooth shape.
Treating the dot plot as a promise.
Quoting taper-tantrum or 2022 numbers without the date window; start and end levels vary by source.
Assuming stress-test scenarios are forecasts; they are severity-calibrated narratives.

claims.text: A DV01-neutral hedge sizes the hedge so the total dollar change per 1bp parallel move is zero; it removes first-order parallel risk only, leaving slope, curvature, convexity and basis risk.
A key-rate-matched hedge sets the hedged book's DV01 near zero at each key tenor (using several instruments), so it also covers non-parallel curve moves up to the chosen buckets.

Futures hedge ratio: contracts = (position DV01 / futures DV01), with futures DV01 ≈ CTD DV01 / conversion factor; equivalently, modified-duration form scales by position MD / CTD MD, times CTD price and CF.
A non-CTD position hedged with CTD-based ratios carries duration-mismatch basis risk; a Eurex example had MD 8.574 vs CTD 7.969 and needed 50 contracts. If the CTD switches, the hedge must be re-run.

Ultra Bond (UB) was launched to give long-end duration the Classic bond contract could not: DV01 more than 50% above Classic at launch; launch basket was narrower (25y+ remaining maturity, verify current spec). Ultra Bond and Ultra 10 saw heavy inflows in 2026, UB open interest up about 20% on average vs 4% for the complex.

Futures-vs-cash basis risk comes from CTD, delivery options and financing; swaps-vs-Treasuries basis risk is the swap spread, which moves with dealer balance sheet limits, liability-driven demand and Treasury supply. A swap hedge of a Treasury position is exposed to swap-spread changes.

Long-end hedge tools in practice: Ultra Bond futures (UB; the brief lists WN alongside it — treat UB/WN as the Ultra Bond/long-end futures pair and verify codes against CME specs), 20y/30y SOFR swaps, and cash bonds; each differs in basis, liquidity and margin/funding.

Mandate constraints enter the optimizer as bounds: cash Treasuries often cannot be shorted (lower bound 0), futures and swaps can take either sign, and desks cap position size, DV01 and gross notional.

Minimizing a quadratic residual-risk term plus an L1 (sum of absolute values) trade-cost term with linear bounds is a convex QP; with an L1 residual only it is an LP. L1 costs encourage sparse trades (few instruments).

cvxpy ships with Clarabel, OSQP and SCS; by default it picks the solver most specialized to the problem class (OSQP for QPs per its docs; Clarabel for SOCPs and default from 1.5 per Clarabel materials). A solver can be forced with problem.solve(solver=cp.CLARABEL).
After solve, check problem.status: 'optimal', 'infeasible', 'unbounded', and '_inaccurate' variants; report infeasibility (which constraints cannot be met) rather than returning a silent best guess.
Futures trade in whole contracts; rounding a continuous solution to integers changes residual risk, so recompute residual DV01 by key rate after rounding. Integer-constrained problems are not convex.

snippets.code:
import cvxpy as cp
w = cp.Variable(n)                    # units of each hedge
resid = A @ w + book                  # key-rate DV01 left over
obj = cp.sum_squares(resid) + lam * (c @ cp.abs(w))
prob = cp.Problem(cp.Minimize(obj), [w >= lo, w <= hi])
prob.solve()                          # or solver=cp.CLARABEL
ok = prob.status == 'optimal'
snippets.note: standard cvxpy API (Variable, sum_squares, abs, Problem, status); not executed here

pitfalls: DV01-neutral looks hedged on paper while a steepener still loses money.
Using the wrong CTD (or ignoring a likely switch) mis-sizes futures hedges.
Swap hedges of Treasury positions add swap-spread risk.
Optimizing without scaling variables (contracts vs notional) makes solvers fail or return inaccurate status.
Rounding after the solve can break limits and key-rate neutrality; re-check.
An infeasible problem must be explained, not hidden; do not relax limits silently.
